Sonali got the design-firm offer this morning, and the whole batch crowded around her. I noticed Gurpreet, her closest friend, hugging her with a wide smile, then standing at the back afterwards, twisting her ID card strap.
Later Gurpreet came to my desk to ask about the next drive. Halfway through, she said, "Can I be honest? I'm happy for her and I also feel really small. We applied to the same firm." She looked embarrassed saying it.
I told her envy is common and can be useful; it often points at what we want. We looked at her portfolio together, and she said what she envied was not the firm but Sonali's confidence in interviews. We booked two mock interviews for next week.
On her way out she stopped by Sonali's bench and said quietly, "You earned it. Treat me to chai?" Sonali laughed and said yes.

So here's the weird part of getting the fellowship, Mehr. Everyone assumes it's all celebration.
Naveen and I applied together. When I got it and he didn't, he said, "Congrats, Madam Scholar," and every time since, it's been a joke. "Oh, you'll be too busy for us now." "Must be nice."

Vikas, you're asking how to be happy for your friend when you're struggling yourself? Let me, your Sabina phuppo, tell you about Reshma.
In 1996 we both applied for the state nursing scholarship in Lucknow. Reshma got it. I didn't. And I was truly happy for her. I sewed her a new kurta for the ceremony and sat in the front row clapping till my hands stung.
But I also went home and cried into my pillow, and told nobody. When Reshma asked, "Are you all right about it?", I said, "Of course! Why wouldn't I be?" For months I felt strangely far from her, and I couldn't understand why.
One day I finally said, "I'm proud of you, and I'm jealous and sad, both." She laughed with relief and said, "Thank God. I thought you were angry and hiding it."
That's when we became close again. So celebrate your friend fully, beta. Just don't pretend you have no other feelings.

qa.a: As a sign Sabina might be angry and hiding it, so she was relieved by the honest answer.

Irawati glanced at her own screen. 71. Her chest loosened, then tightened again. "Seventy-one."

For the third night in a row, Sangeeta came back to the flat in Andheri to find Jaya's dishes in the sink, rice hardening in the pot, and music thumping behind Jaya's door at midnight. Her jaw clenched. She pulled a sticky note from her bag and wrote, "Some of us WORK in the mornings." It was stuck to the fridge before she stopped herself.
Two months of notes and silence, then shouting: that was how her last flatshare had ended.
She peeled the note off and knocked instead. Jaya opened the door, earphones around her neck.
"Can we talk for five minutes? I'm getting really annoyed, and I'd rather say it now than blow up later. Could you wash your dishes by the next morning, and keep the music low after eleven?"
Jaya blinked, then winced. "The pot. Sorry. I didn't realise the walls were that thin."
They wrote two rules on the whiteboard by the door. Jaya added a third: "Sangeeta's coriander is not shared food."

Above the kirana shop in Sirsa, Jaya and Aarti shared a room and a single tap. On Sunday, over the gas stove, Aarti finally said it: "You're hard to live with, Jaya. You tell me off about my slippers, but you use my soap, and you complained about my phone calls to Lalita aunty downstairs."
Jaya's face went hot. She wanted to list every one of Aarti's faults, then go downstairs and get Lalita aunty on her side.
She stirred the dal instead and made herself listen. The soap: true. The complaint to aunty: also true, and she had done it behind Aarti's back.

Aarti nodded slowly. "Calls on the terrace after ten. Your own soap."

Warden's note, Block B, 9 September
Harish came to my office this morning. Over three weeks, 1,200 rupees and a power bank had gone missing from his room. He said the whole floor assumed it was his roommate, because the roommate "is always short of money". But Harish had not accused him. qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Tenzin went to the students' meet?

subtopic: Roommate breaks agreements
passage:
Week one: In the working women's hostel in Hyderabad, Sudha and Ishita discovered they both loved spicy pickle and old film songs. By Friday they were eating every dinner together on the floor of their room, laughing until the neighbours knocked.
Week four: On Saturday Ishita went to her office friends' dinner. Sudha, alone, texted her four times, "When are you back?", and sulked the next morning. Ishita said, "I love our dinners. But I can't be your only person." Sudha felt hurt, then embarrassed, because it was true: she hadn't called anyone else in weeks.
Week seven: Sudha had joined a Sunday pottery class and was slowly getting to know two women from it. On weekday nights she and Ishita still ate pickle and rice on the floor. On Saturdays they each went out, and came back with stories to swap.

qa.q: What did Sudha and Ishita both love?
qa.a: Spicy pickle and old film songs.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after Ishita said "I can't be your only person"?
qa.a: Hurt at first, then embarrassed, realising she hadn't called anyone else in weeks.

qa.q: What did Sudha do to keep the friendship healthy?
qa.a: She joined a Sunday pottery class and got to know new people while keeping the weekday dinners with Ishita.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel about the four texts?
qa.a: Crowded and pressured; she loved their dinners but didn't want to be Sudha's only person.

grounding: Illustrates a warm roommate friendship over weeks and the shift from expecting one person to meet every need to keeping some independence.
